name: Mature cystic teratoma of the ovary

reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: Commonest ovarian germ-cell tumour and the most frequent ovarian neoplasm in young women of reproductive age; usually benign
Contains mature tissue derived from all three germ layers, so cut sections typically reveal sebaceous material, hair, and sometimes teeth or cartilage
Often an incidental finding; when symptomatic it causes vague pelvic discomfort, a palpable mass, or presents acutely with torsion
Ultrasound features are characteristic, including echogenic mural nodules (Rokitansky protuberance), fat-fluid levels, and dense shadowing from hair and sebum
Torsion is the most common complication because of the fatty content and long pedicle; rupture spills irritant sebaceous material and provokes chemical peritonitis
Malignant transformation is rare and almost always squamous cell carcinoma arising in the ectodermal component, seen mainly in older women with larger lesions
Ovarian cystectomy with preservation of normal ovarian tissue is the usual fertility-sparing approach; bilateral disease occurs in a minority
May rarely trigger anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis, so a paraneoplastic neurological presentation should prompt a search for a dermoid
reference.pathophysiology: A mature cystic teratoma arises from a single germ cell that undergoes parthenogenetic development after the first meiotic division, generating well-differentiated tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Ectodermal elements usually predominate, which is why skin, sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and neural tissue are conspicuous, giving the lesion its dermoid character. The tumour is typically a unilocular cyst lined by squamous epithelium and filled with keratin and sebum, with a raised nodule (the Rokitansky protuberance) from which hair, teeth, and other solid tissues project. Because the components are mature, the lesion behaves benignly, with complications arising chiefly from its physical bulk and fatty content rather than from invasive growth.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian fibroma or other solid stromal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to identify fat, hair, and the Rokitansky nodule
Pelvic MRI with fat-suppression sequences when imaging is equivocal
Tumour markers (CA125, AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) mainly to help exclude a malignant germ-cell component
Doppler assessment of ovarian blood flow if torsion is suspected
Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm maturity of all elements
Thyroid function testing if a struma ovarii component is suspected
redFlags: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea suggesting ovarian torsion
Signs of chemical peritonitis following cyst rupture
Rapid enlargement or solid vascularised areas raising concern for malignant transformation
New neuropsychiatric or seizure symptoms suggesting associated anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis
reference.prognosis: Excellent for the great majority, which are benign and cured by complete cystectomy; recurrence is uncommon and usually reflects a new primary. Prognosis worsens markedly if squamous carcinoma has developed within the lesion, particularly when detected late.
pitfalls: Attributing acute pain solely to the mass and missing torsion, which threatens ovarian viability
Rupturing the cyst intraoperatively and spilling contents, provoking granulomatous peritonitis
Assuming all teratomas are benign and overlooking an immature or malignantly transformed component
Failing to consider a dermoid as the cause of a paraneoplastic encephalitis
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Mature cystic teratoma is a benign ovarian germ cell tumour with no FIGO stage and no chemotherapy or radiotherapy role; management is surgical and expectant, not stage directed systemic therapy.

A small, asymptomatic lesion with classic benign sonographic features (echogenic Rokitansky nodule, fat fluid level, dense acoustic shadowing) can be followed with surveillance imaging rather than immediate surgery.
Surgery is favoured for larger lesions, growth on serial imaging, symptoms, or any atypical or complex feature raising concern for malignant transformation or a different adnexal pathology.
Transvaginal ultrasound characteristics drive the decision for operative intervention, with CT or MRI reserved for cases with moderate to high suspicion of malignancy.
The fertility sparing approach is ovarian cystectomy with preservation of normal ovarian tissue.
Oophorectomy is reserved for lesions not amenable to cystectomy, women who have completed childbearing, or when malignancy cannot be excluded.
Adnexal torsion is a surgical emergency; prompt detorsion with cystectomy (if the ovary is viable) or salpingo-oophorectomy (if necrotic) is required.
Cyst rupture with spillage of sebaceous or keratin material causes chemical peritonitis and needs surgical washout plus removal of the cyst.
Malignant transformation of a mature teratoma (usually squamous cell carcinoma) is rare and is managed as the corresponding malignancy, a different pathway from the benign lesion.

If histology instead shows an immature (malignant) teratoma or another malignant germ cell tumour, it is treated with staging and adjuvant platinum based combination chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin), except for FIGO stage IA dysgerminoma and early stage low grade immature teratoma; this applies to the malignant counterpart, not to mature cystic teratoma itself.
Postoperative follow up is by clinical exam and, where indicated, ultrasound to confirm complete excision and monitor the contralateral ovary given the risk of bilateral dermoids.

Routine tumour markers are not required for surveillance since the lesion is benign; markers such as AFP and hCG are used preoperatively to help exclude a coexisting or alternative malignant germ cell tumour when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Refer to gynaecologic oncology when imaging is atypical or complex, malignancy cannot be excluded, the lesion is large or bilateral, or histology raises the possibility of an immature teratoma or other malignant germ cell element.
Acute torsion or rupture warrants urgent surgical referral regardless of the benign nature of the underlying lesion.
